title: The supplier selection process
blurb: Walk through the stages of a typical supplier selection process, and explain why planning the procurement comes first.
question: A hospital needs a new patient-booking system from an external supplier. The sponsor asks the project manager to outline how the supplier will be chosen, from first deciding what is needed to the point the chosen supplier starts work. What stages would a typical process include, and why does planning matter so much?

teach.body: Supplier selection is the process of finding, assessing and appointing the supplier that offers the best value for a defined need. A typical process (organisations name the steps differently) runs from specifying the need and planning the procurement, through going to market and evaluating bids, to negotiating, awarding and managing the contract. Plain English: work out exactly what you want and how you will judge it, then let suppliers compete fairly against that yardstick.

items.label: Identify & specify the need
items.sub: Requirements, specification or statement of work

items.label: Research & pre-qualify
items.sub: Market research, expressions of interest, PQQ

items.label: Invite tenders or bids
items.sub: ITT, RFP or RFQ to the shortlist

items.label: Evaluate the bids
items.sub: Weighted criteria: quality, price, capability, risk

items.label: Negotiate
items.sub: Refine terms with the preferred bidder(s)

items.label: Award the contract
items.sub: Sign, and debrief the unsuccessful bidders

items.label: Mobilise & manage
items.sub: Kick-off, then manage performance and change

teach.caption: A typical sequence, not an APM-mandated list. The order is what exam questions test.

teach.h: Plan the procurement before you go to market
teach.body: Planning settles the procurement route and documents, the evaluation criteria and their weightings, a realistic timetable (allowing for supplier lead times and any rules on timescales), the budget, who sits on the evaluation panel and who approves the award. Fixing the criteria BEFORE any bid arrives keeps selection fair, objective and defensible, and stops the scoring being bent towards a favourite. Poor planning shows up later as vague bids, challenges from losing suppliers and contracts signed late.

teach.caption: Pre-qualification asks 'is this firm capable?'. Bid evaluation asks 'is this offer the best value?'.
Typical usage: organisations use these names a little differently, but all three invite suppliers to bid.

head: Criterion (weight)
Bid A
Bid B
teach.caption: Illustrative only: the exam does not test the arithmetic. Bid A is cheapest, but Bid B gives the better overall value.

teach.body: Northgate Hospital specifies the outcomes it needs: online booking, secure login, accessibility. It plans a 12-week timetable, a panel of IT, clinical and finance staff, and criteria weighted quality 50%, price 30%, risk 20%. An advert draws 14 expressions of interest; a PQQ shortlists five; an ITT goes out; bids are scored; the top bidder negotiates on support terms; the contract is awarded, the other four are debriefed, and a kick-off meeting mobilises the supplier.

In a linear project the requirement can usually be fully specified before tender, so suppliers bid against a detailed specification and price can carry real weight. In an iterative project the requirement emerges, so the specification describes outcomes and priorities, and selection weighs the supplier's capability, agile experience and collaborative fit more heavily. Some buyers add a demonstration or short trial to see how a bidder actually works with users.

teach.text: Classic traps. (1) The ORDER: specify the need and plan BEFORE going to market; evaluate BEFORE negotiating; negotiate BEFORE awarding. (2) Pre-qualification (is the firm capable?) is not bid evaluation (is the offer best value?). (3) The process does not stop at award: unsuccessful bidders are debriefed and the contract is mobilised and managed. (4) Lowest price does not automatically win.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Say it is a typical process, then give the stages in order with a few words on each.
Stress planning: criteria and weightings agreed before bids arrive, so selection is fair and defensible.
Show that evaluation is about value: weighted criteria covering quality, price, capability and risk.
Go beyond award: debrief unsuccessful bidders, then mobilise and manage the contract.
Tie each point to the scenario (what this project is buying, and what would go wrong if a stage were skipped).
A typical process: specify the need, plan, research and pre-qualify, invite bids, evaluate, negotiate, award, mobilise and manage.
Planning fixes the route, criteria and weightings, timetable, panel and approvals before going to market.
Bids are scored against weighted criteria, so best value can beat lowest price.
ITT, RFP and RFQ invite bids; a PQQ shortlists capable firms first.
Iterative projects specify outcomes and weigh capability and collaboration more heavily.

summary: You can now outline the stages of a typical supplier selection process in order and explain what happens at each. You can also explain why the procurement must be planned, with criteria fixed before bids arrive, and how selection differs for an iterative project.

A.q: In a typical supplier selection process, which stage comes FIRST?
A.why: The process starts by identifying and specifying the need. Everything that follows (planning, pre-qualifying, tendering) depends on knowing what is being bought.

whyNot.0: Tenders can only be invited once the need is specified and the procurement planned.
whyNot.1: Bids can only be evaluated after they have been received.
whyNot.3: Pre-qualification needs to know what is being bought, so it comes after specifying the need.

A.q: What is the main purpose of a pre-qualification questionnaire (PQQ)?
options: To shortlist capable suppliers before tendering
To score final bids against weighted criteria
To agree the final price with the chosen supplier
To tell unsuccessful bidders why they lost
A.why: A PQQ checks suppliers' capability, experience and financial standing so that only capable firms are invited to tender.

whyNot.1: Scoring final bids is bid evaluation, which comes after the tender stage.
whyNot.2: The final price is settled through negotiation and award, not pre-qualification.
whyNot.3: Explaining why bidders lost is the debrief, which follows the award.

A.q: In a typical supplier selection process, which stage normally follows the evaluation of bids against weighted criteria?
A.why: After evaluation, the buyer negotiates with the preferred bidder(s) to refine the terms, then awards the contract.

whyNot.0: Pre-qualification happens before tenders are invited.
whyNot.1: Market research is an early stage, before bids are invited.
whyNot.2: Specifying the need is the very first stage.

B.q: Why should the evaluation criteria and their weightings be agreed BEFORE any bids are opened?
options: So suppliers can be chosen on price alone
So selection is fair, objective and defensible
So no supplier ever needs to be debriefed
So weightings can be adjusted to suit a bidder
B.why: Fixing criteria in advance means every bid is judged against the same yardstick, so the decision is fair, objective and can be defended if challenged.

whyNot.0: Weighted criteria usually balance quality, capability and risk with price.
whyNot.2: Unsuccessful bidders are still debriefed after the award.
whyNot.3: Adjusting weightings to favour a bidder is exactly what fixing them in advance prevents.

B.q:
Which THREE of the following are typically settled when planning the procurement?
1) Evaluation criteria and weightings
2) The procurement timetable
3) The name of the winning supplier
4) The procurement route and documents
B.why: Planning sets the criteria and weightings, the timetable, and the route and documents. The winner is only known after evaluation and award.

whyNot.0: Item 3 is wrong: the winner cannot be known at the planning stage.
whyNot.1: Item 3 is wrong, and this option leaves out the timetable.
whyNot.2: Item 3 is wrong, and this option leaves out the evaluation criteria.

B.q: A school needs 300 identical laptops of a set specification and simply wants prices from suppliers. Which document is MOST appropriate to send out?
B.why: An RFQ asks suppliers for a price against a clearly fixed specification, which fits identical laptops.

whyNot.1: An RFP invites suppliers to propose a solution when the way of meeting the need is open, which is not the case here.
whyNot.2: An expression of interest only gauges which suppliers are interested; it does not obtain prices.
whyNot.3: A PQQ assesses supplier capability to build a shortlist; it does not ask for prices.

C.q: A hospital scores two bids. Bid X is 15% cheaper but scores poorly on quality and capability. Bid Y costs more but scores highest overall on the agreed weighted criteria. What should normally happen?
options: Award to X, as lowest price always wins
Rescore Y so that price carries most weight
Recommend Y, as it gives best overall value
Reject both bids and restart the process
C.why: The bids were scored against agreed weighted criteria. Bid Y offers the best overall value, so it should be recommended for award.

whyNot.0: Weighted criteria exist precisely because the lowest price is not always the best value.
whyNot.1: Changing weightings after bids are opened would be unfair and open to challenge.
whyNot.3: There is a clear winner on the agreed criteria, so restarting would waste time and money.

C.q: A council has awarded a contract. The three unsuccessful bidders ask why they lost. What should the council do, and why?
options: Ignore them, as the contract is now signed
Debrief them, for transparency and learning
Reopen the competition so that they can rebid
Share the winner's full pricing breakdown
C.why: Debriefing unsuccessful bidders is part of the award stage. It shows the process was fair and transparent, helps them improve, and reduces the risk of challenge.

whyNot.0: Ignoring bidders undermines transparency and makes a challenge more likely.
whyNot.2: A properly run competition is not reopened just because losing bidders ask questions.
whyNot.3: The winner's pricing is commercially confidential; a debrief explains the bidder's own scores.

C.q: A charity wants an agency to build a donor app iteratively, with features prioritised sprint by sprint. Which evaluation emphasis is MOST appropriate when selecting the supplier?
options: A fixed price for the complete feature list
The lowest day rate, with no other criteria
Proof the agency never changes requirements
Agile skills and a collaborative approach
C.why: In an iterative project the requirement emerges, so the buyer should weigh the supplier's agile capability and how well it collaborates with users.

whyNot.0: A complete feature list cannot be fixed up front when features are prioritised sprint by sprint.
whyNot.1: Price alone ignores capability, quality and risk.
whyNot.2: Iterative working expects requirements to change; refusing change would be a weakness, not a strength.

reteach.title: Booking a wedding photographer
reteach.question: A couple choose a photographer for their wedding. How does what they do follow the stages of a typical supplier selection process?

blocks.h: From 'what do we want?' to the big day
blocks.body: First they agree the date, style and budget (specify the need) and what matters most: style, then price, then reviews (plan the criteria). They browse portfolios and ask friends (research and pre-qualify), then ask a shortlist for quotes (invite bids). They compare quotes against their priorities (evaluate), agree an extra hour for the evening (negotiate), book one and politely tell the others (award and debrief), and send the shot list before the day (mobilise and manage).

steps.label: Decide what matters most
steps.sub: Style first, then price, then reviews

blocks.text: The couple decided what mattered most BEFORE seeing any quotes. If they had picked their criteria afterwards, they would just be justifying a favourite. That is why planning the criteria comes first.

explain.body: First define what is needed (a specification or statement of work). Then plan: the route and documents, criteria and weightings, timetable, panel and approvals. This is the yardstick every bid will be measured against.

test.q: A project team agrees the procurement timetable, the evaluation criteria and their weightings before contacting any supplier. Which stage are they in?
test.why: Setting the timetable, criteria and weightings before going to market is planning the procurement.

whyNot.1: Evaluation applies the criteria to bids, which have not arrived yet.
whyNot.2: Mobilising happens after the contract is awarded.
whyNot.3: Negotiation happens after bids are evaluated.

explain.body: Research the market and invite expressions of interest. A pre-qualification questionnaire (PQQ) shortlists capable firms. The shortlist then receives the tender documents (ITT, RFP or RFQ) and submits bids.

test.q: Which document formally invites shortlisted suppliers to submit a priced bid for the work?
test.why: An invitation to tender (ITT) formally invites suppliers to submit a bid.

whyNot.0: An expression of interest is the supplier saying it is interested, before any tender.
whyNot.1: A lessons learned log records experience, not bids.
whyNot.3: A benefits profile describes a benefit, not a supplier bid.

explain.body: Bids are scored against the pre-agreed weighted criteria (typically quality, price, capability and risk). The buyer then negotiates with the preferred bidder(s) to refine terms before award.

test.q: Why are bids typically scored against weighted criteria rather than on price alone?
options: Price is never relevant to selection
It balances quality, capability and risk
It lets the panel ignore any weak bids
It removes the need for negotiation
test.why: Weighted criteria balance price with quality, capability and risk, so the buyer chooses the best overall value.

whyNot.0: Price is relevant: it is usually one of the weighted criteria.
whyNot.2: Every compliant bid must be scored fairly, not ignored.

explain.body: The contract is awarded and signed, and unsuccessful bidders are debriefed. The supplier is then mobilised (kick-off, access, plans) and the contract is managed for performance, changes and payment.

test.q: Once a contract has been awarded, what is the final stage of a typical supplier selection process?
test.why: After award, the supplier is mobilised and the contract is managed through to completion.

whyNot.0: The strategy is written before selection begins.
whyNot.1: Pre-qualification happens before tenders are invited.
whyNot.2: Market research is one of the earliest stages.
